intro_en: The Israel National Trail passes among the hills of the northern Negev, with scenic lookouts, a green agricultural area and a wonderful winter bloom.
character_en: Gentle, with easy climbs over the hills. The walk is on dirt roads exposed to the sun
transport_en: At the turn-off to Moshav Ahuzam, a little north of Tel Keshet. Devira Interchange. The entrance to Kibbutz Dvir
pois_en: Nahal Sad canyon. Tel Nagila. Pura Nature Reserve
important_en: After rain, the section between Tel Nagila and the Pura Nature Reserve is a little difficult to pass, and your shoes may get wet.
description_en:
From Road 40, south of Moshav Ahuzam, we climb 300 metres north-west to Tel Keshet. This is a relatively small tel where remains of a Bronze Age settlement were found.
The trail continues west on a jeep track that is also marked blue. After about 3 km we descend south on a red-marked trail. After 3 km on the red marking, the trail turns sharply left and after a short distance reaches Nahal Sad. If you missed the sharp turn and reached the blue-marked scenic road, keep walking and after 1 km you will reach the southern side of the Sad canyon, where you can walk there and back and enjoy the beautiful surroundings.
The Nahal Sad canyon is one of the most beautiful and surprising sections in the area. The trail passes east of it, above the narrow channel of the stream that cuts into the rock and forms one of the few canyons in the northern Negev. In late winter and early spring the bloom is wonderful and there is water flowing in the stream. Above the canyon there is a trail library.
At the end of the canyon the trail continues east along the 'blue' scenic road, to the foot of the hill of Tel Nagila (Negila on the map). From here we climb to the finest lookout in the area.
A few words about Tel Nagila: finds at the site date from the Chalcolithic period (about 5,000 years ago) up to the Byzantine period. On top of the tel there are archaeological excavations that only 'professionals' can make sense of. But besides these there are also 'pirate' excavations, prompted by a special story from the days of the First World War, a tale that some believe to be true. Soldiers in a battalion of the Ottoman army collected an especially large sum of money, which they took with them as they fled from the British army advancing northwards in its conquest. During the retreat, they decided to bury the money in a place that would be easy for them to find after they defeated the British and regained control of the area. A tree standing on top of the tel (which has since collapsed) was chosen as the marker, and beneath it, according to the story, they buried the treasure. To this day it is not known whether the treasure was found, or whether it was ever buried at all. But there are still those who try to dig for it and find it.
In early March thousands of white asphodels bloom here. There is a good wooden deck for resting, taking in the view and, of course, coffee. If visibility is good you can look out to Mount Hebron in the east and over the whole northern Negev and the southern coastal plain. The area around the tel is surrounded by wheat fields, and a little west of here is the Kibbutz Ruhama area with the beautiful badlands around it.
A few words about the Nahal Shikma Scenic Road named after Ariel Sharon: the 'blue' road is a KKL-JNF initiative to connect Road 40 and the Pura Nature Reserve with the Ruhama area, and from there to the sea near the mouth of Nahal Shikma, a route 45 km long. The road is passable for any vehicle, although after rain the passage in certain sections may be challenging. The road passes by the Sycamore Farm (Havat HaShikmim) and Anemone Hill (Givat HaKalaniyot), where Lily and Ariel Sharon are buried, and it is named after him. Note: on Saturdays, the section between the Pura Nature Reserve and the Sad canyon may be very crowded with vehicles.
From Tel Nagila, the trail descends north-east and curves to the south-east. We cross a small channel, a tributary of Nahal Shikma, where there may be minor passability problems. If necessary, improvise a bridge with stones or branches, or take off your shoes for a moment. In February, look nearby for a lovely concentration of mandrake flowers.
We proceed a little further east and reach the embankment of the old Turkish railway. This is a good spot for a short rest and a view. Remains of the railway embankment can also be seen in the Beersheba area, in Nahal Revivim south of Mashabei Sadeh and especially in the Tel Nitzana area (more on Wikipedia).
The trail continues east in the only section of this segment that passes under the shade of trees, a large KKL-JNF grove between the railway line and the Pura Nature Reserve. The trail leaves the trees and meets the 'blue' road, only to leave it again and walk through the most flower-filled and best-known section: the Pura Nature Reserve. On weekends the reserve is crowded with flower lovers, but the trail is wide and there are enough flowers for everyone to photograph.
Next to the parking area beside Road 40, you will probably meet 'Gazlan' with a good shakshuka. From here we continue 3 km south and then turn left under the road through a culvert. The trail continues south, and after 6 km curves east. At the bend you can cut south towards Road 3255 (Devira-Lahav Junction) and go to the Alonit convenience store to stock up on water and food.
From the bend we proceed about 5 km east, passing north of Kibbutz Dvir (Devira on the map; both names are correct). The segment ends at the entrance to the kibbutz cemetery. We turn right off the trail onto a kurkar (sandstone) road, walk about 400 metres to the road and a little west alongside it, and reach the bus stop at the entrance to the kibbutz.
nearby_en: 'Yaldudes' bakery in Kiryat Gat: not within walking distance, but about a 10-minute drive from Tel Keshet you will find a wonderful place, the 'Neve Hanna' children's village, which runs the 'Yaldudes' quality bakery (check opening hours on Google; it is worth calling ahead). An opportunity to buy healthy and excellent breads and crackers, made by the children who live in the village (in Waze: Neve Hanna, Kiryat Gat).
A memorial in Kiryat Gat to those who perished during the Ethiopian aliyah, marking a painful subject that is not often spoken about.
Rahat municipal market: a short drive into the city from the entrance near Shoval. Cheap food and clothing and other bargains in the largest Bedouin city in the country.

Winter bloom in the Ruhama Badlands Nature Reserve: the 'blue' scenic road continues west from Nahal Sad and reaches an enchanting area of kurkar hills, small cliffs and a vast abundance of winter flowers, with anemones and much more. It can also be reached from the direction of Kibbutz Ruhama.

Philip's Farm (Havat Philip): those driving on Road 6 miss it, since access is only for those travelling from north to south on Road 40. A lovely spot for a rest, buying a saj pita with a variety of toppings and other good things, and of course toilets. It is an opportunity to hear from the locals about Philip, who founded the farm in the 1950s (in the days when Sharon was establishing the Sycamore Farm).
author_en: Omer Shapira, Hikes Coordinator, Tourism Division, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI)
